verdict: NEGATIVE RESULT. Integrity scores annotator-labelled camera visibility at AUROC 0.569 against 0.571 for object range alone -- a difference of -0.001, which is not a difference. The map does not predict object visibility better than one number already available for free. The pre-stated hypothesis that it would work for low objects and fail for tall ones is also unsupported: no height band beats its own range baseline. What DOES hold up is the occlusion term, worth +0.0416 AUROC within the integrity score itself, so ray-casting camera visibility adds real signal even though the construct it feeds does not clear the baseline. The reading: this map measures GROUND-PLANE observability, and ground-plane observability is not object visibility -- a car behind a car has an occluded footprint and a perfectly visible roof. It should be presented as an observability prior for planning, not as a predictor of whether an object will be seen.
caveats: Visibility labels describe the OBJECT; the integrity score describes its GROUND FOOTPRINT. A tall van visible over a low wall is a genuine disagreement, not an error, so perfect agreement is not expected.
Labels are annotator judgement in 4 coarse buckets, not a measurement.
Per-camera trust is held at the constant 0.795 for every camera: no faults are injected here, so this tests the geometry and occlusion terms, NOT the learned trust head.
Boxes beyond 45.0 m are excluded -- coverage weight there is near zero for every camera, so the score has no dynamic range left.
nuScenes mini is 10 scenes from 2 cities; this is not a broad generalisation claim.
Four scoring variants were tried (footprint mean, max, p90, and front-edge cell). All landed between 0.495 and 0.551, i.e. all null. Reported so the mean is not mistaken for a tuned choice.
